newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: UK's CDC aims for Ivorian rubber start-up in 1998.
newsitem.headline: UK's CDC aims for Ivorian rubber start-up in 1998.

text.p: British buyers of a rubber estate in Ivory Coast said on Thursday leases holding up construction of a processing factory should be granted in July, allowing initial output of 6,000 tonnes a year from mid-1998.

Britain's privatised Commonwealth Development Corporation, a former state overseas development group, bought the Cavally estate from the Ivorian government in March 1996 for 2.6 billion CFA francs ($4.5 million).
It has since been waiting for the government to grant a promised 60-year land lease for the 7,500-hectare site before factory construction, CDC and plantation spokesmen told Reuters.

"There is a good chance the factory will be ready by June 1998," Compagnie Heveicole de Cavally Finance Director John Stevens said in an interview, adding that profitability was expected in late 1998 -- six months later than planned.
The factory complex, costing around four million pounds and with an initial rubber output capacity of 6,000 tonnes, rising to 12,000 by 2002, had originally been planned for late 1997.

"By the end of July we will have reached the three months (public) consultation period for the lease," which had been due last September after approval of site boundaries, Stevens said in Ivory Coast's commercial capital Abidjan.
CDC (Ivory Coast) director Abou Kone said Cavally faced a battle against wet season weather to complete factory building and accommodation.
"We will have 72 kilometres of swampy approach roads. That will probably cut us off until November," he said.

Until then, Cavally would process its rubber through two other privatised rubber firms close to the growing southwestern port of San Pedro -- SAPH (Societe Africaine de Plantations d'Heveas) and SOGB (Societe des Caoutchouc de Grand Bereby).

Cavally also faced heavy security costs. Ivory Coast's nearby western border with Liberia was declared an "operational zone" under military plans announced last July to crack down on gangs alleged to be arriving with refugees from Liberia's war.
"It's a worry," said Stevens, pointing to armed guards for convoys to and from the site even before construction begins.
He said Cavally was well placed to benefit from rising world demand for natural rubber and had already sold to French tyre manufacturing giant Michelin.
CDC has also expressed interest in financing other Ivorian interests already sold or about to be put on the market -- including rubber, sugar, telecommunications and energy firms.
"But it is very time-consuming to obtain a lease on land," he said.
